title: Orff v. United States (2004 Ninth Circuit)
lead: Farmers benefiting from a federal water-delivery contract tried to enforce it after allocations were cut to protect listed fish. The Ninth Circuit concluded that the contract did not give them direct enforcement rights and vacated merits rulings entered without a sovereign-immunity waiver.

actors.name: Individual Westlands landowners and water users
actors.role: Farmers pursuing claims after the district withdrew its complaint.

actors.name: Westlands Water District
actors.role: Party to the 1963 federal water-delivery contract.

actors.name: United States and Bureau of Reclamation
actors.role: Federal contracting party and agency administering water deliveries.

actors.name: Judge Clifton
actors.role: Author of the Ninth Circuit opinion joined by Noonan and Thomas.

proceedings: The district court first ruled on several merits claims, then reconsidered beneficiary status and dismissed for lack of a waiver. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the jurisdictional conclusion but vacated the earlier merits adjudications. Each party bore its own appellate costs.
limits: This narrative concerns only the February 18, 2004 Ninth Circuit stage. It does not resolve all allocation legality, establish a trust relationship, or combine later appellate decisions. Possible other-forum remedies and an unappealed separate Barcellos ruling remained outside review.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A district secures federal water for its landowners
sections.cue: What did the 1963 contract and later settlement establish?
paragraphs: Westlands Water District received San Luis Unit water from the federal Central Valley Project under a 1963 contract with the United States. Individual landowners and users benefited from deliveries but were not parties to that district-government agreement.

In 1978 the Government asserted that the contract was invalid. Litigation ended in a 1986 stipulated judgment in Barcellos upholding the agreement and requiring federal performance. That earlier judgment later figured in the farmers’ effort to establish their own authority to sue.

sections.title: Species protections lead to a reduced allocation
sections.cue: What earlier contract ruling framed the new dispute?
paragraphs: The Sacramento River winter-run chinook salmon was listed as threatened in 1990, and the Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta’s delta smelt received that designation in 1993. The responsible federal agency determined that continued project operation jeopardized the species. Under the Endangered Species Act and Central Valley Project Improvement Act, the Bureau of Reclamation cut Westlands’s 1993 allocation to fifty percent of its contracted supply.

Earlier litigation construed Article 11(a) to relieve the United States from liability for a shortage caused by statutory mandate, while allowing a separate challenge to the merits of statutory compliance. That interpretation supplied background, not a merits determination of every allocation issue in this appeal.

sections.title: The farmers continue the suit after Westlands withdraws
sections.cue: How did the district court reach and then reconsider jurisdiction?
paragraphs: Westlands began the present action in May 1993. Farmers and the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) intervened. Westlands dismissed its complaint without prejudice in 1995, leaving the farmers to file a second amended complaint.

On June 5, 1998, the district court dismissed statutory claims for lack of Tucker Act jurisdiction, noting possible proceedings in the Court of Federal Claims, and rejected the theory that reclamation statutes themselves were contracts. Remaining claims concerned appropriative water rights, trust obligations, contractual and constitutional surcharge challenges, and breach of the 1963 agreement. The farmers said water and trust rights were incorporated into that contract.

The court initially treated them as a contracting entity within 43 U.S.C. §390uu’s waiver. It granted Government summary judgment on the first three remaining groups but found triable contract issues. On April 12, 2000, reconsideration under Klamath Water Users Protective Association v. Patterson led it to classify the farmers as incidental beneficiaries and find no waiver. Final judgment for the Government entered August 1. The farmers appealed; Westlands returned as an intervenor to protect its interests, and it and NRDC filed briefs.

sections.title: The earlier litigation does not preclude the immunity defense
sections.cue: Why did Barcellos and the McCarran Amendment not resolve jurisdiction?
paragraphs: Judge Clifton, writing with Judges Noonan and Thomas, reviewed immunity and subject-matter jurisdiction anew. The United States needed an express waiver, strictly construed in its favor.

Barcellos I had addressed alleged action beyond agency authority and the McCarran Amendment’s water-rights waiver. This suit alleged no such ultra vires action and sought private damages, not comprehensive adjudication or administration of all claimants’ rights on a stream. The issues were not identical. The 1993 allocation also arose from species listings after the earlier case, creating a different factual transaction and defeating claim preclusion.

The McCarran Amendment did not cover this private dispute. Even considering administration of previously adjudicated rights, the farmers identified no specific adjudicated right violated here, instead asserting rights implicitly incorporated into the contract. General earlier adjudication did not make this a comprehensive proceeding. Their pleaded waiver was §390uu rather than the McCarran Amendment.

sections.title: Benefit from a government contract does not itself confer an enforceable right
sections.cue: What did the statutory waiver require?
paragraphs: Section 390uu permitted joining the United States as a necessary defendant to adjudicate contractual rights of a contracting entity and the Government under reclamation contracts. The farmers claimed intended-third-party-beneficiary status brought them within that language.

Klamath required clear contractual intent to grant government-contract beneficiaries enforceable rights. Individuals need not be named if they belonged to an intended class, but even express mention of that class did not alone establish direct enforcement rights. A water project could knowingly benefit farmers without making them parties entitled to sue on the district’s agreement.

Article 15 required payment of district assessments or charges before receiving water, even if an assessment had been found irregular or void. It also required district-user agreements to subordinate supply to the federal contract. Those were conditions for obtaining water through Westlands, not a direct relationship with the United States.

Article 11(b) limited shortage relief to a payment adjustment and referred to the district or those claiming through it. The payment concerned money Westlands paid the Government. The broader wording could cover an assignee succeeding to district rights and duties in contractual privity. These farmers had no such assignment.

sections.title: The panel acknowledges another circuit’s different beneficiary approach
sections.cue: Why did other contracts and the settlement still not supply a waiver?
paragraphs: The Ninth Circuit expressly noted possible disagreement with H.F. Allen Orchards in the Federal Circuit. It understood that decision to rely on beneficial use and ultimate payment without examining particular language. To the extent that was the rule, this panel respectfully disagreed and required clear intent in the specific contract.

The farmers also held separate recordable agreements with the Government concerning excess-acreage land, including ten-year sale obligations, valuation, and eligibility. Article 5 made water receipt subject to the district contract, while only excess-land Articles 23, 24, and 25 were directly incorporated. The farmers sued on neither those provisions nor another term of their own agreements. Contracting status under one instrument did not permit enforcement of different obligations in another.

The Barcellos stipulation and judgment expressly disclaimed being a contract or amendment for §390uu. Participation therefore did not establish the required status. A separate district ruling concerning damages over $10,000 under that judgment and a possible Court of Federal Claims route was not challenged on appeal and remained unreviewed.

sections.title: An assumed trust relationship does not overcome the missing enforcement conditions
sections.cue: Why were the earlier merits decisions vacated?
paragraphs: The panel did not decide whether Westlands was the farmers’ trustee. Even assuming it, the farmers neither sought judicial compulsion against Westlands nor alleged the Government directly participated in a trust breach, as required by the exception invoked to sue in the trustee’s place. That theory supplied no demonstrated basis here.

Without a waiver, the district court lacked authority from the outset. Its earlier belief that jurisdiction existed could not preserve merits rulings after recognition of the defect. The appropriative-rights, trust, and surcharge decisions were vacated as nullities binding neither this case nor others.

Bell v. Hood’s distinction between jurisdiction and failure to state a federal claim did not alter that result. The defect was absence of sovereign consent, not merely inadequate allegations on the merits.

sections.title: The jurisdictional dismissal stands, but the merits adjudications do not
paragraphs: On February 18, 2004, following argument February 11, 2003, the Ninth Circuit affirmed in part and vacated in part. It upheld the conclusion that no immunity waiver permitted these farmers’ claims and removed the earlier substantive rulings. Each party bore its own costs, and no separate opinion was issued.

The judgment awarded no damages and did not hold that every disputed reduction complied with every duty. Nor did it foreclose every conceivable proceeding in another forum. It resolved this appeal’s waiver problem and the consequences for rulings made without jurisdiction.
